rejected.title: Sustainable harvesting by First Peoples
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have cared for Country for tens of thousands of years. Over that time they built deep ecological knowledge: knowledge of how plants, animals, water and seasons fit together.
This knowledge was passed on through stories, songs, ceremony and teaching from Elders. It guided how and when resources were harvested.

Harvesting practices include taking only part of a resource, so enough is left to regrow or breed. Another practice is following the seasons, harvesting a plant or animal only when it is plentiful and not breeding.
Practices differ between Nations because each Country has its own plants, animals and climate. Sustainable harvesting means using a resource in a way that lets it last for future generations.
rejected.remember: Knowledge of Country guides what is taken and when, so the resource lasts.

a.q: Why does taking only part of a resource help it to last?
opts: Enough is left to regrow or breed
Plants and animals no longer need to grow
The resource can be harvested at any time
Other resources are used up in its place
a.why: If some of the resource is left, plants can regrow and animals can breed, so there is more to harvest later. Harvesting at any time is not the reason, because the card says practices follow the seasons.
a.clue: Think about what is left behind after harvesting.

b.q: A community harvests a river fish only in the months when it is not breeding. Which idea about sustainable harvesting does this show?
opts: Following seasons, so breeding is not disturbed
Taking only part of a resource from each place
Using one fixed practice across every Nation
Passing on knowledge through written reports
b.why: Harvesting only outside the breeding months is following the seasons, so the fish can breed and the population lasts. Taking only part of a resource is a different practice: it is about how much is taken, not when.
b.clue: The scenario is about when the fish is taken, not how much.

version.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander sustainable harvesting
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples built deep ecological knowledge over thousands of years: how the plants, animals, water and seasons of their Country are linked.
This knowledge guides harvesting so a resource lasts. One practice is taking only part of it, such as some eggs from a nest, so enough is left to breed or regrow.
Another practice is following the seasons: a plant or animal is harvested when it is plentiful and left alone while it breeds. Signs such as a plant flowering can show when the time is right.
Practices differ between communities, because each Country has its own plants, animals and climate.
version.remember: Ecological knowledge guides how much is taken and when, so the resource is still there later.

a.q: Why does leaving part of each yam in the ground help the yams last?
opts: The part left behind can regrow into new yams
Yams left in the ground stop other plants growing
The yams can then be dug up at any time of year
Leaving part of each yam makes the soil dry out
a.why: Taking only part of a resource leaves enough to regrow, so there are yams to harvest again later. Digging them up at any time of year goes against following the seasons.
a.clue: What happens to the part that stays in the soil?

b.q: A community catches a kind of fish only after a certain tree flowers, which signals the fish have finished breeding. Which practice does this show?
opts: Following the seasons, using signs from nature
Taking only part of the fish from each river
Catching the fish whenever people need food
Using the same rule as every other community
b.why: The flowering tree is a seasonal sign, so the fish are caught after breeding, when taking them does less harm to the next generation. Taking only part of a resource is about how much is caught, not when.
b.clue: Is this about how much is taken, or when?
